newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN finds kids with machete, bullet wounds in Zaire.
newsitem.headline: UN finds kids with machete, bullet wounds in Zaire.

text.p: The U.N. Children's Fund on Tuesday reported a rise in the number of Rwandan Hutu refugee children with bullet and machete wounds in rebel-held east Zaire amid mounting allegations of violence by its Tutsi-dominated troops.
Spokeswoman Marie Heuze stopped short of say the rebels had butchered children, but accused them of blocking relief work so as to put blame for the chaos on the "whole U.N. system".
At least 80 of 230 Rwandan refugee children found on Sunday at Biaro, south of the rebel-held city of Kisangani, bore bullet and machete wounds, according to Heuze.
"An enormous number of children have been wounded by bullets and machete and we can't treat them," she told a briefing.
Heuze said rebel troops were preventing her agency from bringing in medical supplies to treat serious injuries.

"Rebel troops are preventing us from treating these children on the spot," she told Reuters. "Our nurses report that they have no supplies and are simply able to pick out worms from the infected wounds which are already days old."

Pamela O'Toole, spokeswoman for the U.N. refugee agency, expressed deep concern over "reports of human rights abuses and even killings" in areas south of Biaro. Rebels have not given its staff access to Rwandan refugees there.

Heuze said authorities of the rebel Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) admitted that their soldiers abducted 52 children and 10 adults on April 26 from the hospital at Lwiro, north of the eastern city of Bukavu.
"They've recognised their responsibility in a precise text," she said. The abduction was due to "an absence in communication" between the civilian officials authorities and the military.
The 52 children, handed over to UNICEF by rebel authorities at Bukavu airport four days later, have been repatriated to Rwanda. "Ten of them are between life and death," Heuze said.
"Obstacles to our humanitarian work at Kisangani are being multiplied," Heuze said. "That is why the Security Council meeting in New York is so important to us, so we can work in correct conditions."
UNICEF hoped the Security Council, convening later in New York, would pass a firm resolution calling on the rebels to stop hampering humanitarian operations, according to Heuze.

Asked why the rebels were placing obstacles, Heuze replied: "It is to prevent our work from being done. It is to put the responsibility for the disorganisation on the back of the whole U.N. system," she said. "It is very clear.
"We can't do evacuations like refugees were cattle. We can't push people into trains and planes in unspeakable conditions.
"A minimum (standard) must be respected. We are there to uphold that minimum with our mandate to protect."
The Hutus are the remnants of two million Rwandans who fled to Zaire after Tutsi rebels ended the Hutu-led genocide of minority Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994.
Many among them killed or watched others kill in one of the worst mass slaughters of the century.

Sadako Ogata, U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees, voiced frustration over refugee rescue efforts in remarks in Washington on Monday. She blamed a breakdown in coordination with local authorities for the death of some 100 Rwandan refugees in a packed train on Sunday.
O'Toole said that following an accord with local authorities, UNHCR staff would accompany trains in the future.

Heuze, referring to the area near Biaro where the 80 wounded children were found, said UNICEF believed between 5,000 and 6,000 children were in the jungle there. Nine-hundred children had been returned to Rwanda so far.
